paragraphs: “‘That is what the first question in the wilderness meant. That is what You turned down, for the sake of the freedom You placed above everything else. Yet the great secret of this world lies hidden in that question. Had You chosen “bread,” You would have met the one need all humanity has, always—the need to find someone to worship. A man who is free has no goal he pursues so restlessly and so painfully as this: to find someone to worship. But he wants to worship something no one can dispute, something so plainly established that all men would agree at once to bow to it. These pitiful creatures are not satisfied to find what this man or that man can worship. They must find something that everyone will believe in and worship, and above all they must do it _together_. This craving for worship in _common_ has been the chief misery of each man, and of the whole race, since time began. For the sake of common worship they have put each other to the sword. They have set up gods and challenged one another: “Put away your gods and come and worship ours, or we will kill you and your gods!” So it will be until the end of the world, even when the gods have vanished from the earth. They will fall down before idols all the same. You knew this basic secret of human nature. You could not help knowing it. Yet You refused the one sure banner that was held out to You, the banner that would have made every man bow down to You alone—the banner of earthly bread. You refused it for the sake of freedom and the bread of Heaven. Now see what You did next. And again, all of it in the name of freedom! I tell You, no anxiety torments man more than the need to find, and quickly, someone to hand over to the gift of freedom with which the poor creature is born. But only one who can quiet their conscience can take their freedom from them. In bread You were offered a banner nothing could beat: give men bread and they will worship You, because nothing is more certain than bread. But if someone else gets hold of man’s conscience—oh! then he will throw away Your bread and follow the one who has trapped his conscience. In that You were right. The secret of man’s existence is not just to live, but to have something to live for. Without a firm idea of what he lives for, man would not agree to go on living. He would rather destroy himself than stay on earth, even with bread in plenty. That is true. But what came of it? Instead of taking men’s freedom away, You made it greater than ever! Did You forget that man prefers peace, even death, to the freedom of choosing in the knowledge of good and evil? Nothing tempts man more than his freedom of conscience, and nothing makes him suffer more. And now see: instead of building a firm foundation to put man’s conscience at rest for ever, You chose everything that is exceptional, vague and puzzling. You chose what was wholly beyond men’s strength, and acted as though You did not love them at all—You, who came to give Your life for them! Instead of taking over men’s freedom, You added to it. You loaded the spiritual kingdom of mankind with its sufferings for ever. You wanted man’s love given freely. You wanted him to follow You freely, drawn and made captive by You. In place of the rigid ancient law, man would now have to decide for himself, with a free heart, what is good and what is evil, with only Your image before him as a guide. But did You not know that in the end he would reject even Your image and Your truth, once the fearful burden of free choice weighed him down? In the end they will cry out that the truth is not in You. They could not have been left in worse confusion and torment than You have left them in, piling on them so many cares and so many problems that have no answer.

“‘So in truth You Yourself laid the foundation for the ruin of Your own kingdom, and no one is more to blame. And yet, what was it that You were offered? There are three powers, only three, that can conquer for ever the conscience of these helpless rebels and hold it captive, for their own happiness. Those forces are miracle, mystery and authority. You rejected all three, and You gave the example for rejecting them. The wise and dread spirit set You on the pinnacle of the temple and said to You, “If You would know whether You are the Son of God, throw Yourself down. For it is written: the angels shall hold him up so that he does not fall and hurt himself. Then You will know whether You are the Son of God, and You will have shown how great Your faith in Your Father is.” But You refused. You would not throw Yourself down. Oh, of course, You acted proudly and nobly, like God. But the weak, unruly race of men—are they gods? Oh, You knew then that if You took a single step, made a single move to throw Yourself down, You would be tempting God and would lose all Your faith in Him. You would be smashed against the very earth You came to save. And the wise spirit who tempted You would have been delighted. But I ask again: are there many like You? Could You believe for a single moment that men, too, could stand up to such a temptation? Is human nature made so that men can turn down miracle? In the great moments of their lives, the moments of their deepest and most agonizing spiritual struggle, can they hold only to the free verdict of the heart? Oh, You knew that Your deed would be written down in books and handed on to distant ages and to the farthest ends of the earth. You hoped that man, following You, would hold to God and ask for no miracle. But You did not know that when man rejects miracle, he rejects God as well. Man looks not so much for God as for the miraculous. And since he cannot bear to be without the miraculous, he will make new miracles for himself. He will worship acts of sorcery and witchcraft, even if he is a hundred times a rebel, a heretic and an infidel. You did not come down from the Cross when they shouted at You, mocking and insulting You, “Come down from the cross and we will believe that You are He.” You did not come down. Again You would not make man a slave by a miracle. You longed for faith given freely, not faith founded on miracle. You longed for free love, not for the base raptures of a slave before a power that has terrified him for good. But in this You thought too highly of men. They are slaves, of course, though rebels by nature. Look around You and judge. Fifteen centuries have gone by; look at them. Who have You raised up to Yourself? I swear, man is weaker and baser by nature than You believed! Can he, can he do what You did? You showed him so much respect that You seemed to stop feeling for him, for You asked far too much of him—You, who have loved him more than Yourself! Had You respected him less, You would have asked less of him. That would have been closer to love, because his burden would have been lighter. He is weak and vile. So what if he is now in revolt everywhere against our power, and proud of his revolt? That is the pride of a child, of a schoolboy. They are little children rioting and locking the teacher out of the classroom. But their childish delight will come to an end, and it will cost them dearly. They will pull down temples and soak the earth in blood. But in the end they will see, the foolish children, that though they are rebels, they are rebels without strength, who cannot even keep their own rebellion going. Drenched in their foolish tears, they will recognize at last that He who made them rebels must have meant to mock them. They will say so in despair, and what they say will be blasphemy, which will make them more unhappy still. For man’s nature cannot bear blasphemy, and always ends by taking its revenge on itself. And so: unrest, confusion and unhappiness—that is the lot of man today, after all You suffered for the sake of their freedom! The great prophet tells, in vision and in image, that he saw all those who shared in the first resurrection, and that there were twelve thousand from each tribe. But if there were so many, they must have been not men but gods. They had carried Your cross. They had lasted scores of years in the barren, hungry wilderness, living on locusts and roots. And You may indeed point with pride to those children of freedom, of free love, of free and glorious sacrifice for Your name. But remember that they were only a few thousand. And what of the rest? How are the other weak ones to blame, because they could not endure what the strong endured? How is the weak soul to blame, if it cannot take in such terrible gifts? Can You really have come only to the elect, and only for the elect? But if so, that is a mystery, and we cannot understand it. And if it is a mystery, then we too have the right to preach a mystery. We have the right to teach them that what counts is not the free judgment of their hearts, and not love, but a mystery that they must follow blindly, even against their conscience. That is what we have done. We have corrected Your work and built it on _miracle_, _mystery_ and _authority_. And men were glad to be led like sheep again, and glad that the terrible gift that had brought them such suffering was at last lifted from their hearts. Were we right to teach them this? Speak! Did we not love mankind, when we humbly admitted its feebleness, lovingly lightened its burden, and, with our sanction, let its weak nature sin? Why have You come now to get in our way? And why do You look at me so silently and so searchingly with Your gentle eyes? Be angry. I do not want Your love, for I do not love You. And what is the use of hiding anything from You? Do I not know Whom I am talking to? Everything I can say is already known to You. And is it for me to hide our mystery from You? Perhaps You wish to hear it from my own lips. Listen, then. We are not working with You, but with _him_—that is our mystery. It is a long time now—eight centuries—that we have been on _his_ side and not on Yours. Exactly eight centuries ago, we took from him what You rejected with scorn: the last gift he offered You, when he showed You all the kingdoms of the earth. From him we took Rome and the sword of Cæsar, and we declared ourselves the only rulers of the earth, though to this day we have not managed to finish our work. But whose fault is that? Oh, the work is only beginning, but it has begun. It will be a long time before it is done, and the earth still has much to suffer. But we shall triumph and be Cæsars, and then we shall plan the happiness of all mankind. Yet You could have taken the sword of Cæsar even then. Why did You reject that last gift? If You had accepted the mighty spirit’s last advice, You would have achieved everything man looks for on earth. That is, someone to worship, someone to keep his conscience, and some way of uniting everyone in one agreed and harmonious ant-heap. For the craving for universal unity is the third and last torment of men. Mankind as a whole has always struggled to set up a world state. There have been many great nations with great histories. But the more highly developed they were, the more unhappy they were, because they felt the craving for world-wide union more sharply than other peoples. The great conquerors, the Timours and Ghenghis-Khans, swept over the face of the earth like hurricanes, trying to subdue its peoples. They too were only the unconscious expression of that same craving for universal unity. If You had taken the world and Cæsar’s purple, You would have founded the universal state and given the world peace. For who can rule men, if not the one who holds their conscience and their bread in his hands? We have taken the sword of Cæsar. In taking it, of course, we have rejected You and followed _him_. Oh, there are ages still to come of confused free thought, of their science and their cannibalism. For they began to build their tower of Babel without us, and they will end, of course, in cannibalism. But then the beast will crawl to us, lick our feet and spatter them with tears of blood. And we shall sit upon the beast and raise the cup, and on it will be written, “Mystery.” But then, and only then, the reign of peace and happiness will come for men. You are proud of Your elect, but You have only the elect, while we give rest to all. And besides, how many of those elect, those mighty ones who might have become elect, have grown tired of waiting for You? They have carried, and will carry, the strength of their spirit and the warmth of their heart over to the other camp, and they end by raising their _free_ banner against You. You Yourself lifted up that banner. But with us everyone will be happy. They will no longer rebel or destroy one another, as they do under Your freedom. Oh, we shall persuade them that they will become free only when they give up their freedom to us and submit to us. And will we be right, or will we be lying? They will be convinced that we are right. They will remember the horrors of slavery and confusion to which Your freedom brought them. Freedom, free thought and science will lead them into such difficulties, and bring them face to face with such wonders and unsolvable mysteries, that some of them, the fierce and rebellious, will destroy themselves. Others, rebellious but weak, will destroy one another. The rest, weak and unhappy, will crawl to our feet, fawning, and whine to us: “Yes, you were right, you alone possess His mystery, and we come back to you, save us from ourselves!”
